utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning Mr. Tieger. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to raise quickly two matters. First, I also wanted to add to the expression of gratitude to the Bench and particularly to Judge Lattanzi for sitting late last night in order ensure that the witness can leave as needed. I also wanted to add that in light of those efforts, we consider it highly unlikely that it is necessary to have an extended sitting today, and thereby further inconvenience the court personnel and also unnecessarily result in Judge Lattanzi's absence in order to complete the witness given the allocated or projected times. So we would suggest that we revert to the original schedule, concluding at 1.45. If for some reason we haven't concluded with the witness by that time, then we obviously have the option to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. I think it's fair enough. Any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And secondly, looking at the schedule over the next two days, I think it's clear, based on the -- on our experience and the projected times that we'll be lucky to conclude the next three scheduled witnesses by the end of the week, and in -- and even in the unlikely event that we were in a position to commence with Witness 122, it would only be the very beginning of his testimony. In light of that, could we, for a number of logistical reasons, ask the Court for a bit of predictability and simply have confirmation that Witness 122 will commence on Monday so he doesn't need to be brought here needlessly and repeatedly? I've also discuss that with Mr. Robinson as I did the previous matter, and I believe he agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough, too, given that I'm not sure whether we can surely finish Mr. Ristic this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Unless there are any other matters, we'll bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Alan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we begin -- well, first of all, I should have you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Robert Djurdjevic. It's not as scary to pronounce as it looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll keep that in mind for the transcript and for the proceedings. I'd like to begin by calling up what we have termed 65 ter 22306, which is the sworn interview that was conducted on the 18th of December, 2002. While we're waiting for that to actually come up on screen, let me begin by -- actually, I see it now. I believe you've had a chance to review the transcript of that proceeding during which you were interviewed by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor. Can you confirm, Mr. Djurdjevic, that it actually reflects the statement you gave at that time, that that information was true and correct to the best of your knowledge, as reflected by the fact that you were sworn at that time, and that if asked about the same matters again here in court you would provide the same information.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is I have reviewed it, and I stand by it. It is accurate as best as I can remember both then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 22306 and the associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we'll admit the interview as 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4513, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the associate exhibit. It has only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will also be admitted as Exhibit P4514.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll offer up a quick summary and then we'll move on to the -- some additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, I'm just going to very briefly and quickly summarise some of the information in the statement for benefit of the public, which doesn't have it before them, and then I will move on to some additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, during the conflict, the witness met on numerous occasions with various Serbian and Bosnian Serb political and military leaders including the accused on a number of occasions. He kept a detailed record of these meetings in various trip diaries, portions of which were sometimes used as a basis for publications in the witness's newsletter and later a web site. On the 14th of July of 1995, the witness met with the accused. Immediately prior to his meeting with the accused, Mr. Karadzic had been meeting at length with Miroslav Deronjic and a delegation from Srebrenica. During the witness's meeting with the accused the discussion also focused on Srebrenica as well as Zepa. During that meeting, the accused disparaged what they were watching on CNN and Sky News, utilised large maps in his office showing various army placements to refer to Srebrenica and Zepa and explained that the military strategy involved driving things to the boiling point. During their meeting, the accused received a call from a field commander who was defending the major road north of Srebrenica, a call about fighting around Konjevic Polje and Kasaba. That concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, I know some of your background is encompassed in the interview, but perhaps I can just touch on that briefly. Is it correct that you were born and raised in Serbia, graduated from the University of Belgrade in 1968, and then came to North America, that is, first Canada and then the United States in 1970?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone and speak directly into it. The interpreters are having difficulty to hear him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You are probably hearing at the same time. And please put a pause between the questions and answers, please. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You became involved and quite successful at business, and then in 1989, you became re-involved with the former Yugoslavia; first having contact with and becoming friendly with President Milosevic, beginning by offering business-related advice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition with the advent of the conflict, is it correct that you became concerned about reporting in the mainstream media and began writing yourself in defence of the Serb position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I had reluctantly stepped into those shoes because, frankly, when I left Yugoslavia or former Yugoslavia, as it was known then, in 1970, I never suspected that I would ever be coming back, and I had pretty much erased that name from my life, because of the issues I had with Communists at the time and the reason I left. And I had not gone back for almost 20 years, and it wasn't really until my wife kept putting these clippings of the Western press in front of me and asking me to corroborate the stories repeatedly that I finally and reluctantly decided to look into it on my own and see where the truth is. That's how that first trip took place in 1989 and then led to many others over the next 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those efforts eventually took the form of a web site called Truth in Media as a platform for articles?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That was my communications vehicle when the internet became available to -- through which to publish the -- my findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you just alluded to the numerous trips you took to the former Yugoslavia, and during those trips, as indicated in the interview, is it correct that you met with many Serbian and Bosnian Serb political and military leaders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And also many others, like, for example, the foreign ambassadors in Belgrade. I would always stop by and meet all of the major powers first before I would go into the field trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you record those meetings contemporaneously in various trip diaries referring to those specific trips?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I did, religiously, because even though I have to say I've been gifted with a pretty good memory, I found it important to record everything almost verbatim as I could remember it as soon as the meeting or an event had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that the diary entries summarised the meetings and various aspects of the meetings that you had, sometimes paraphrasing what people had said and sometimes quoting them verbatim?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Both -- both statements are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as you noted in your interview of 2002 and also in the associated exhibit, you met with Mr. Karadzic on July 14th, 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was during a trip that is reflected in a journal called "War Drums are Beating," covering a trip from the 5th of July to the 31st of July; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did that trip start?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously from my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I mean where did you first arrive in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's see if I remember. Back then we were still under the embargo so I would have to have gone through Hungary, flown to Hungary, probably, and then gone by land, meaning by land travel, from Budapest to Belgrade. Then I remember I had gone to Montenegro first. I believe my daughter was with me at the time, so I dropped her off at my sister's place in Montenegro, and then I came back to Belgrade from where I picked up this trip to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you, therefore, had a number of meetings before your meeting with Mr. Karadzic on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I did, in Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, one of those meetings was with Momcilo Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And could I call up, please, 65 ter 06972, page 9 of the e-court. Okay. And if we could turn back to the previous page very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see the header there meeting with General Momcilo Perisic, Chief of Staff -- Chief of General Staff, Yugoslav army and the time and place. That's a reflection of the meeting that I just asked you about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page, please. Now, here you're indicating a portion of your discussion with Mr. Perisic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Perisic. And we see a graph here, the source of which we see is General Perisic. What does that graph depict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: As I recall, the graph depicts the military budgets of the Serbian - meaning Yugoslav, I think they were still calling themselves Yugoslavs at the time - army and versus their enemy in wartime, the Croats in this case, and the point that -- that General Perisic was making -- he was actually appealing to me to organise some sort of financial help for the -- from the diaspora, from the Serbs living abroad, to help out with the war effort and to -- in support of that plea, he was sharing some of these figures. He said that the Croatian military budget was 5.3 billion as composed to -- as compared to Serbia's 2.6, but more importantly, that the trend was up as far as the Croats are concerned and drifting downwards as far as the Serbian budget is concerned. So that's what those two lines reflect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it a correct understanding of what he was conveying to you and what the chart indicates that the positions, the relative strength of the military in 1991 and 1992 was that the Serbs were much stronger, the Serb strength was declining, the Croat and Muslim strength was increasing, and that at some point just after 1995 they would converge, and that trend would continue to the disadvantage of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what this chart communicates and that's what he communicated as well. He said at the moment we're still stronger but if the trends were to continue, then the enemy would get the upper hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he also speak with you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, now, you can continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry not to remind myself to pause. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did General Perisic also speak to you about the relative impact or lack of impact of the sanctions that had been imposed? And in that regard, could we turn to the next page in e-court. Mr. Djurdjevic, looking at that first paragraph, is that a reference to your discussion with General Perisic about the -- how -- about what effect the sanctions had or did not have?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If it pleases the Court, may I clarify something here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Mr. Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this would be a good place to explain my methodology, if you'd like, in keeping these notes and conducting these interviews. As you can see from this paragraph, General Perisic told me that this has to stay between us. In other words, sometimes the person I'm communicating with, usually the head of state, head of the army would confide in me and share confidential information for reasons that they only know why, but if they prefaced it with this way, it would stay between us and I would always honour that. And for that reason, these diaries that you're now looking at had been under embargo for I believe a period of five years at the Stanford University archives because I did not want them in my discussions with the chief protagonists of the Balkans wars in any way to affect the outcome of those wars. And so what we're now looking at is an after-the-fact recount of a historical record. In other words, I had honoured what he had asked me to do and did not publish any of that information. It only came out into the public domain for the first time in 2002 when I had that interview with the investigators of this court, and they had previously -- they told me they had previously gone to Stanford University to look up these records and read these diaries because the embargo had elapsed. So I thought it would be important for you to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Djurdjevic. Can we see the first page of this diary. We see there -- is it your handwriting at the bottom part, "Until three years after the Yugoslavia --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three years. Yeah, I thought it was maybe five. But, yes, that is my handwriting and my initial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, back to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thank you for the explanation, Mr. Djurdjevic. Back to that portion of your discussion with General Perisic. Did he indicate to you that the sanctions had not affected the support by the Yugoslav army for the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and I recall being very surprised by it because I knew that the United Nations monitors were posted on the border, and so I asked him, So how did you get around those, and replied something, like, you know, We leave that discussion for after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender those two pages and I'll also be making other references so I presume we can add to those as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit -- yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there's some irrelevant material in that interview with Mr. Perisic -- or General Perisic, so I would prefer that we just admit those portions of the pages that have been discussed in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the convenience, we'll admit those two pages, and the Chamber will have no reference to other part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless it is raised later on by any other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We get the message, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, I want to move on to your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That was Exhibit 4515 and the new 65 ter number will be 06972A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, I want to move on to your meeting on the 14th of July. Is it correct that you crossed into Bosnia on the 13th of July via Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now -- and I may refer back to at least one of the meetings you had prior to that meeting, but let me move on to the meeting now. You mentioned at pages 22 through 23 of the 2002 interview that you spent most of the afternoon, from about noon onwards, in Mr. Karadzic's office and saw various comings and goings including a delegation led by the person who was or was supposed to be the appointed mayor of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I call up again 65 -- the previous exhibit, that is 65 ter -- what's the new 65 ter -- well, previous 65 ter 06972, and specifically page 35 of the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There we see a reference to the meeting with Dr. Karadzic and the time, I believe you make clear, you ultimately got in but also a reference to the fact that throughout the afternoon Dr. Karadzic had been meeting with the mayor designate of Srebrenica, Miroslav Deronjic, and other people from there, that is Srebrenica, who were supposed to constitute the civilian authority in the newly liberated area. He apologised - he meaning, I take it, Dr. Karadzic -- apologised for having kept me waiting but he said this was pressing government business for the RS. And is that an accurate reflection of what you recorded at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, did you know by that time something about Srebrenica and specifically did you know by that time whether or not the civilians from Srebrenica, that is the Muslim civilians from Srebrenica, were gone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that people -- that I have -- that I was talking to say that. I never made it to Srebrenica, you know, to see for myself, but, yes, I did hear several people tell me that by the -- by that day, July 14th, Muslim civilians had been evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can -- in that connection, can we turn to e-court page 28, which reflects a portion of your meeting the previous day with Professor Koljevic. I'm going to direct your attention to the top of this page. But just so you can orient yourself, perhaps we can turn to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We're now the day before and my meeting with Dr. -- Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay. And now if we could --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn down to the bottom of the page. There's a reference to a proposed visit of Dr. -- of Professor Koljevic to Srebrenica. And now turn to the next page, please. And there we see the entry, "But one of the phone calls shattered this plan. ZM ...," and can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That was the Chief of Cabinet for Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "ZM took the call, then put the receiver down when he was finished. 'There are no civilians left any more,' ZM announced, 'Mladic had shipped them all out already.'" Does that accurately record what you learned on that occasion about what had transpired in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, when you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender these pages as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be added to the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, when you finally made it into Mr. Karadzic's office for your meeting on the 14th, what was the main focus or topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually we had covered a lot of ground during this meeting that lasted probably at least two hours, but the -- obviously the focus was on Srebrenica. That was the news of the day, and for much of the meeting Dr. Karadzic had been watching the Western media reports about that which were being displayed on two TV screens. I don't mean that he was being disrespectful. He would often mute the sound so we could have a conversation while the reporting went on, but every once in awhile when something looked interesting he would stop the conversation. We would watch to see what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Djurdjevic, just by way of courtroom dynamics, you will sometimes find me pausing. That's to allow the translation in French to catch up.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I've got that. I've experienced this in translations, foreign languages, especially with Japanese, taking a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with the focus on Srebrenica, did Mr. Karadzic tell you whether the actions in Srebrenica had resulted from an order, and if so, did he name or describe the order?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating that? I missed the introduction to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. I -- I just referred to the fact that the discussion was about Srebrenica, and, in light of that, asked if Mr. Karadzic had told you whether the military action in Srebrenica had resulted from an order, and, if so, did he name or describe the order, and perhaps I can turn your attention to page 39 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The answer is yes. And, yes, he did say that. He described it as his order number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And here we see the entry under "Current military situation," covering this particular portion of your meeting on the 14th of July. The diary entry is: "RK said that the attacks on Srebrenica and Zepa were a part of what he called 'my order number 7.' He said that their objective is 'to raise the temperature to the boiling point.'" And then he went on to talk about his expectations or concerns about what the Croats might do in the Krajina to relieve pressure on Bihac.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. And to me, the latter one was really the most significant part of that statement because it foretold the future, actually. That did happen some weeks later in August of 1995. It was quite a prescient comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this -- this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 39 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct? I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djurdjevic, you indicated that in addition to explaining that the attacks were part of "my order number 7," Dr. Karadzic told you that the objective was to raise the temperature to the boiling point. Did you hear a similar reference or similar references from other Bosnian Serb leaders as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and, in fact, it struck me interesting that I heard it from three top civilian leaders of the country: First, Dr. Koljevic, then President Karadzic, and then later on also from the speaker of the parliament, Mr. Krajisnik. So I concluded from that they were all speaking in one voice, that they were all on board with the same strategy, and I remember wondering -- I wondered where it originated, who was a follower and who was the leader in this thought process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to direct your attention to those references in just a moment, but in connection with your comment about speaking in one voice, can I turn your attention to 65 ter 23639, e-court page 10. This is from a trip diary that was entitled "War on Ice." And that reflected a trip from November 28th through December 5th, 1995. And if we could just move down the page slightly. There you record at the bottom of that entry regarding Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic a comment by Professor Koljevic: "The international community thinks that because I speak English well and have taught Shakespeare at American universities I am somehow different that Karadzic or Krajisnik ... that's nonsense. I believe in the same things as Karadzic or Krajisnik." Is that an accurate -- that's unquote, by the way. Is that an accurate reflection of what Professor Koljevic told you at the time, and was that consistent with your experience with him overall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes and yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be added as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Djurdjevic, I indicated I would bring you to the references that you had alluded to a few moments ago. First, can we turn back to 65 ter 06972, at page 29, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could we remain on this page a bit. Mr. Djurdjevic, what -- what did you understand it to mean when Koljevic said they will have to go, and what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now in December of 1995. It was the time of what is now known as the Dayton agreement being formulated and signed. For all intents and purposes, the war was over, and I believe that Professor Koljevic was making a statement about how do we, meaning the country, go forward from here and that he was expressing his opinion that the two heads of state, one head of state, the other one head of the army, were no longer suitable for the period that was ahead for the peacetime leadership in the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then how did you understand the same thing when he said he believed in the same thing as Karadzic or Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that he was talking there about his ideology, about his belief in the right of the Serbian minority, in the Bosnian Serb Republic to do the same thing that other parts of the former Yugoslavia have done, to secede, to have their on country, to make their own decision, to exercise their rights to sovereignty, because that was the reason that these three people, specifically Dr. Karadzic, Professor Koljevic and Mr. Krajisnik ended up in the leadership positions at the outset of the war. They were not professional politicians. All of them were almost cajoled into these roles, kind of reluctantly stepped into it, just like -- reluctantly [indiscernible] became a war correspondent under the need -- press of the needs that the nation had at the time. They answered their call, and they found themselves to be ideologically on the same page. That's what I believe he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And again, if we could turn back to 65 ter 06972, to page 30 of the e-court. Looking at the last entry on that page, Mr. Djurdjevic, is that a reference to bringing the war to a boiling point made by Mr. Koljevic, in -- who also said -- who also predicted the end of the war in one to two months, six months at the outside?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we could also turn to page 46 of the e-court. You had also made a reference to Mr. Krajisnik talking about raising the temperature to the boiling point. And if we could scroll down a little bit farther under the section "War's end," we see the entry: "As was the case with NK," presumably meaning Nikola Koljevic, "and RK," Radovan Karadzic, "MK," Momcilo Krajisnik, "also talked about raising the temperature to the boiling point." And also continued to indicate that his assessment, as we saw also with Professor Koljevic, was that the war would end in one or two months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, and those both accurately reflect what you were told and what you recorded contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I had also alluded to a few minutes ago when I said that I heard these three things in three different meetings, three different individuals using the same terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender those pages, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. They will be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, in your interview in 2002 and in the associated exhibit, you refer to the phone call that Mr. Karadzic received from the field commander, the large maps with the military positions, his reference to his order number 7. With regard to Mr. Karadzic as a military commander and -- had you noted in previous visits his interest and detailed involvement in military matters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: At times I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to 65 ter 23637, page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, this is an entry from your trip diary of May 22nd through 31st, 1994, a trip you entitled -- or the trip diary you entitled "When the going gets tough, the tough get going." And if we can turn to the previous page, we can see the bottom of at that page. The entry begins with a conversation that Mr. Karadzic is having on the phone during which he says: "Don't worry about it. The winners always write the history of war. We will be the winners, that's for sure." Now we continue on to the next page: "There's absolutely no doubt about it so just carry on, et cetera." And then you continued to describe what you had heard during the course of your visit that day. As you describe it: "As I listen to RK," that is Radovan Karadzic, "speak all day as if he were an expert military commander," quote, now quoting Dr. Karadzic, "'we'll take this hill here, this road there, we'll give up this town,' et cetera," he would say. And then you offer some observations about your concerns about his military background and ability to serve as a military strategist. In any event, I wanted to ask you if that accurately reflects what you heard on that occasion during your meeting with Dr. Karadzic first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it does, and as you can see, for the benefit of the Court, in italics the comments made in italics really reflect my opinions. So you can kind of regard that as kind of editorial comment, if you like, rather than parts of the conversations that I've had. And as -- as you can see from those notes, I was wondering just where and, you know, what the point of that was; and then kind of musing also, considering how our top military strategist botched up the war in Vietnam, for example, perhaps it is best that nonprofessionals do lead the armies rather than professionally trained army officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And I can turn to the page but perhaps you and the Court and the Defence will accept my representation or confirm it that this is a meeting of May 27th, 1994, which began, according to the entry at page -- page in the hard copy, page 24, began at 11.40 and actually went from 11.40 to 18.15 with Dr. Karadzic's wife, Ljilja, attending the luncheon part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with that, Mr. President, I would tender that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, those two pages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted. We give the separate number for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll give a number per article.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be fair enough. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that event, 65 ter 23639 will be Exhibit P4516, and 65 ter 23637 will be P4516 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure transcript -- could you confirm the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 23639 will be Exhibit P4516, and 65 ter 23637 will be Exhibit P4517.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjevic, I want to leave that July meeting and ask you about three additional meetings, two of which took place during the same July 1995 trip and one of which was on a different trip. First, is it correct that on the same day you met with Dr. Karadzic, you almost immediately, before you went to his office, you also met with Aleksa Buha, the Foreign Minister of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 32 of 06972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm confused with our 65 -- did we see 65 ter number 23639 at all, "War and ice"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that was used, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page was used?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would have been page 10. I don't know if we used it -- another page for context, but it was page 10, I believe. I think we only used that page. That was a reference to Professor Koljevic explaining that his views were the -- or positions, attitudes, are the same as Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the exhibit number for 6972 was Exhibit P4515; correct? Not 16. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see, Your Honour, you're both Registrar and the Chief Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies. It was confusing. Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, at the bottom of that page we see a reference to your meeting with Mr. Buha, and if we could turn to the next page. There we see a discussion about the Contact Group plan, that is Mr. Buha raising with you the issue of the Contact Group plan, and explaining to you that according to him, the US special negotiator Charles Redman had drawn a map that had Doboj -- gave Doboj to the Muslims and did so according to Redman to ensure that the Serbs would reject the plan. First of all, is that an accurate reflection of what Mr. Buha told you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall if, at that time or any other time, Mr. Buha suggested any other reasons why Doboj might have been designated as a Muslim area or falling within the authority of the Muslim authority other than an effort to foil the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe we discussed it at all except in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you happen to know the pre-war demographics of Doboj, that is whether it was a Muslim majority area or a Serbian majority area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I still don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, although I don't see a reference here and so I think I know what the answer is, did Mr. Buha explain to you why it would foil or scupper the plan if the Serbs didn't get Doboj?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't explain. I just assumed it was a town important to the Serbs. For what reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djurdjevic, I wanted to ask you if you learned during the course of your various meetings with political and military officials that at least in some areas or on some occasions Muslim villages had been razed by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that. The answer to that question would be yes. As far as any warring party is concerned, I've heard stories from all sides alleging that Muslim or Serbian or Croat villages for that matter have been razed by the opposing forces, but specifically I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me assist, if I may then. If we could turn to 65 ter 23636, page 7. First of all, perhaps -- let me indicate to you and we could turn back two previous pages. This is an entry from September 10th, 1993, and it begins with your trip to Bosnia from Belgrade with Dr. Karadzic's personal driver and security guard, and then the conversation continues from there. And I wanted to bring your attention to the excerpt two pages away under "Churkin Church" on page 7 of the e-court. That's it. And there we see RC, that is Dr. Karadzic's driver, saying that he showed Vitaly Churkin, the Russian special representative -- some of the Muslim villages were completely razed during the fighting, and in addition, showed Churkin a pile of rubble and said, Look what they did to our church. And then you learned from him that, in fact, that was a mosque not a church. First of all, is that an accurate reflection of what you learned from him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give the separate number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and, finally, I'd like to turn back to what is either, I think, P4515, but, in any event, is 069 -- was previously 65 ter 06972, at page 48. And again if we could turn back a page. Just so you can see, Mr. Djurdjevic, that's a meeting with Colonel Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who that was, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe he was head of the intelligence services for Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and do you recall during that meeting that Colonel Salapura indicated to you when, in his view, the war would be over? And perhaps we can turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: If you can let me do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And see the entry at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Quoting Colonel Salapura: "This war will not be over when some politicians sign a peace treaty. This war will end when one of the three nations in Bosnia becomes extinct. We have to make sure we're not the one." Does that accurately reflect what Colonel Salapura told you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender that page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be added to Exhibit P4515.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And that, Mr. Djurdjevic, concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we, in total, admitted his article or part of article, from one, two, three -- five items, including the associated exhibits? Four, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. That refers to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Because we have some aggregated references. I think that would be right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. We have about more than 15 minutes until we have the first break. Can you start now. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you and Mr. Tieger for meeting with the Defence. I hope this will help us to conclude very briefly. I'd like to start with the latest item. On page 25 today, Mr. Tieger showed you that the driver carried out something that was silly around the church and the mosque. He did something silly. But did the Muslims and Croats destroy Serbian mosques, and did they destroy the [indiscernible] Tomic monastery at the beginning of the war? According to the knowledge you have, wherever they took a village or a town of some kind, did they destroy our churches?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to wait for the end of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness will not -- the interpreters were not able to catch up with you because you started while interpretation was going on. So one tip is to look at the transcript. When the transcribing is over, that's the time you can start, or you use the microphone in English, but I'll leave it to you, Mr. Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it okay if I answer in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely, there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I guess -- I'll get the timing right eventually. Dr. Karadzic, my answer is: Yes, I've heard stories, said earlier, of all warring parties, all three warring parties, destroying each other's churches, villages, in the course of the war, and that includes the Muslims destroying the Serbian churches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you gain the impression that the destruction of churches or the unnecessary destruction of villages was part of a civil war, of personal vendettas, or was your impression that these were the policies that I was, in fact, pursuing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, I have never heard you condone any such acts. More often than not, when we would have our conversations, I've heard you condemn any militant actions that were not directly focused on the military objectives in a given campaign. So, no, at no times have I heard you encourage; on the contrary, I've heard you condemn any acts of violence against your enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They asked you about Doboj. I'd like to ask you the following: If I tell you that the Serbs formed a relative majority in Doboj, together with the Yugoslavs at the time, were, on the whole, only Serbs, and they were a significant majority, if I tell you that Doboj is a link to a large Serb population on the Ozren mountain, does this, to you, seem to be a significant factor for the survival of Republika Srpska? Would you consider Doboj to be of significance for the survival of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: As I have said before, I got the impression that it was important to the Serbs. I just didn't know why. So thank you for explaining it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know when municipalities are referred to this does not necessarily mean the entire municipalities? And the Serbian side took into consideration the fact that the Muslim part of a municipality might belong to a Muslim constituent entity -- or, rather, municipalities in the course of the war were divided along the confrontation line. It doesn't mean that the Serbs had control over an entire municipality. They had control, on the whole, over the Serbian parts of a given municipality.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I have followed the war more from a macro-standpoint than from the micro-viewpoint, and frankly, I'm not familiar with the territory or the counties enough to know the difference and the boundaries between this or that ethnic group in each county.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about military skills, would you agree that in every country the president or the leader has strategic command, strategic control, over the army? And my thoughts about returning territory, towns, my thoughts about negotiations, is one of a president's prerogatives.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think in any civilised country that I know of, the military is subject to civilian rule; and, therefore, in your wartime situation, you were the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you correctly noticed, I haven't got a military education or background. Did you gain the impression that the tactical and operative matters were dealt with by the army, but the political leadership only dealt with strategic issues when it was necessary to negotiate; for example, when it was necessary to try and put an end to the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's a difficult question to answer with a yes or no answer, because as you know, I have been following this war for many years and have seen a number of situations in which the wishes of the civilian leadership conflicted with those of the military command. I do know that -- I remember having conversations with the military leaders, Mladic in particular, and some other generals who were frustrated at times to have to follow the civilian rule and sometimes stop, for example, a military campaign to allow you and others in the civilian government to negotiate probably some sort of a diplomatic solution rather than try to solve everything on the ground through fighting. So I'm not sure where I would draw the line between strategic and tactical involvement of the civilian government, and that's why I'm saying it's a difficult question to answer. I guess in the wartime conditions, I'm thinking back in our country, World War II, other wars that have been fought. I'm sure that there had been times that President Roosevelt and Churchill and so -- similarly what may have seemed like tactical decisions, and yet they were civilian leaders. So as I said, this is a bit of a grey area as to where the jurisdiction of the civilian government ends and the military begins and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you heard from some of us that things should be brought to a head, did you take this to mean that our intention was to act in such a way to bring things to a boiling point in order to put an end to the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that you -- all of you, all of your civilian leaders, believed that at the time. I also recall a conversation I had the night before we met on July 14th with Professor Koljevic in which he shared with me an anecdote about his brother, who I believe was a playwright or something like that, being invited to a reception in Belgrade. And at that reception, the representative of Her Majesty's government of Britain allegedly said to Professor Koljevic's brother that Her Majesty the Queen would not have any problems if the Serbs resolved the situation militarily on the ground. Now, this conversation had taken place before the attacks on Srebrenica and Zepa. So obviously Professor Koljevic concluded that this was a kind of a kind of a green light being given by Britain for the Serbs to engage in the military solution that would bring the war to a quick end. To me, at the time, this felt like a trap that ultimately you saw as well and foresaw, because it had only escalated the war at one end in order to give the enemy advantage on the other side -- on the other side, the Krajina in the southern part of the Bosnian Serb Republic. And that led to what is now known as Operation Storm, which ultimately did lead to both the end of the war and NATO's involvement through bombing in August and I believe September of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to remind you of something that General Perisic told you, namely that we were still stronger, but that if this continued we would lose. Do you agree that given that Yugoslavia was under sanctions and that Republika Srpska was under even worse sanctions, the Republika Srpska could not accept the war continuing for a long time, because if they did so that would mean we would fail, if we accepted the war continuing as it had done for three and a half years up until that point in time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe and have said that many times in our conversations between you and I and many other leaders that I've spoken with that the time is not the friend of the Serbian interests. The time is on the side of the enemy, and that the longer the war lasted, the more advantage your opposition will gain. That chart that General Perisic talked about, and that later on I reproduced, merely reflects that in a graphical way how militarily the opposing forces would strengthen both internally and externally through weapons that were being shipped to them. And therefore the longer the war lasted, less of a chance would be for the Serbian side to prevail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since you read English, Mr. Djurdjevic, could you take a look at the transcript and supplement what's missing from there. I remember you started with "I remember" something, something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said I remember that in the conversations between you and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjevic. Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic -- or, I note the time. If it is convenient, we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As you like it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For 20 minutes. We will resume at 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, do you agree that the assessments that I had that I shared with you at the time, according to which the Croats would attack Krajina through Bosnia, according to which the war would come to an end in two and three months' time, did all these assessments of mine, in fact, prove to be correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you were right. As I said, you were very prescient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to remind you of a conversation with Professor Koljevic in December. Do you agree that as early as November 1995, as early as the 21st of November, the Dayton agreement was concluded and it stated that those who were accused would not be able to hold official positions? Was that the basis for Koljevic's request that Ratko Mladic and myself should leave our positions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That may well have been the reason for his opinion. I cannot speak for him. I don't know what his reason was. Personally, I was not aware of that provision, and so I just -- I cannot speculate, really, as to what he may have thought and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But now that you know that that was a provision of the Dayton agreement, it seems more reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a pointless question. Just move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Excellency, the witness initially thought that Koljevic thought that wartime leaders wouldn't be appropriate leaders for peacetime. That's why I put this question to the witness, but the basis for the question is a legal basis. It relates to the indictment. But very well, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the course of our meeting, you said that I monitored the reporting of some leading international channels, and when I asked you in the interview whether this was a semi-private, a semi-official meeting at which we would watch things together, when -- you, in fact, said that when I watched those leading international channels, the only sort of information I could obtain would be misinformation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is true. That is why, in fact, I felt the need to continuously visit the country where the war was being fought, so that I would not get disinformed, so that I would have a chance, first-hand, to find out what the full truth is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you said that I could only obtain false information, does that mean that the conclusion you drew was that the media was not conveying the truth, but, rather, that they were biased, and they were biased against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: There's no question about that. There's no question that I believed that then and I do believe it now, and that that was the reason that I originally and subsequently got involved in direct reporting the part of the truth about the war in the Balkans that the American public and the Western public in general had not seen from the mainstream media which at times I jokingly called the lame-stream media. And, Your Honour, if I may say, the reason for the non-profit organisation under which I reported my findings from the war, "Truth in media," was not chosen lightly. And similarly, the reason I'm here as a voluntary witness, I have been told by the US attorney before I gave that deposition in 2002 that as a member of the media, under the US law I cannot be subpoenaed, but I volunteered to be here. And some of you may wonder why I gave up the sunny beaches of Hawaii to come here in the dead of winter, but the reason is that what I said to you at the outset: That I'm here to speak the truth and nothing but the truth is not just an oath for me. It's the very same reason why I travelled through wartime conditions, because that is actually my sole purpose, and that is my sole commitment. So for that reason, I've also counselled at times Dr. Karadzic when he asked me for opinions about the Western media, what can or cannot be believed, because I found that often times disinformation was passed on to the American public and other Western public not by outright lying but the deception by omission, by omission of the salient facts, and I saw it as my mission to fill in these gaps so the full truth be known. Because without the full truth, there cannot be a full reconciliation, and without the reconciliation, there cannot be real peace and harmony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjevic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've been living in the democratic world for years. You went there because you objected to the previous system in place. You are, so to speak, part of the diaspora. Do you agree that the diaspora condemned Milosevic's sanctions on the Drina against Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I can say the diaspora speaks with one voice. I can say for myself that I have condemned that, that I had seen that. I perceived that as a sign of betrayal of the common interest and the common good by Milosevic. And I'm not aware of any public statements by the diaspora per se, because as I said I don't think there's such thing as one voice in which the diaspora speaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I had the majority of the diaspora in mind. The reason for putting this question to you is the following: Did General Perisic have any reasons -- or, rather, could he consider this attitude of the diaspora to be an indication that the sanctions weren't in force or that it was possible to bypass the sanctions in some way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I cannot speculate as to General Perisic's motives for making that statement. What you're saying seems plausible. What I can say is that I got a distinct impression that he was cultivating or was in a good relationship with the military part of your state, of the Bosnian Serb Republic, specifically Mladic and the military leaders, and was actually speaking disparagingly of you and the civilian leaders. I recall him saying at one stage that the biggest mistake that Milosevic had made was when he agreed to have Karadzic head up the Bosnian Serb Republic, things like that. He also accused you of some other improprieties that seemed pretty far-fetched, that even the Bosnian Serb military leaders that I spoke to had discounted. But there was clearly no love lost, I would say, between Perisic and yourself and other civilian leaders of the Bosnian Serb Republic, and he was trying to give me an impression that he was still in very good relationship with the military part of the Bosnian Serb Republic despite the sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During that and previous visits, were you able to observe that there was this ideological rift within the body of the Serbian people? It was very much alive, and the left and the right had frequent frictions. Could you view what Perisic told you in that light? Could you put it in that context as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be a fair assessment. It has been my observation that by and large the military leadership of all factions that I have met with was still pretty much Communist -- leaning toward the Communist ideology. They were trying to adjust to a new environment in which there was no longer Soviet Union and the world power -- polarity of the two world powers, but they were still thinking with the Red Star on their foreheads. And I had actually witnessed with you in our discussions in earlier meetings several situations which highlighted that. I remember, for example, you telling me a story on one of those trips, it was before 1995, I would venture to guess maybe it was that one in September of 1993, about an incident in which the Serbs, the Serbian Army under General Mladic, had made advances, I believe it was on Igman and Bjelasnica, when they were conducting an offensive toward Sarajevo, and that's when you ordered them to stop so that you could -- you and other civilian leaders could engage in diplomatic negotiations and try to come up with a solution in a peaceful way. And you were lamenting the fact that Mladic had apparently signed a cease-fire agreement with the, I guess, Muslims - I guess that's who they were fighting at that point at that location - and had then advanced anyway, and you were really angry, miffed at him, because you said to me that when a Serbian officer gives his word of honour, that has to be the word of honour. And the Communists have never word what it means to have honourable agreements, and so you were very angry that he had -- you said you were not angry that he had taken the territory that he did, but that he should have concluded his military campaign first and then signed the cease-fire agreement, rather than sign the cease-fire agreement, break it in order to grab more land. So that's just one example that comes to mind where this Communist ideology: The power, might makes right. The power -- military power rules had clashed with your beliefs as a political leader of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 23638, page 4, where you discuss the very Mount Igman episode. The bottom part. Page 4 in hard copy. This seems to be page 8 in e-court, but in hard copy it's page 4. Yes, we have it. At the bottom, does this part relate to what you said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before I look at the details, would someone please tell me what meeting and what time-frame we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's a meeting with Sloba Mamlic, Major. It's on the next page. The date was the 13th of May, 1996; that is to say, following everything.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm looking at here is Srebrenica and Zepa. That's not what I was talking about. I was talking about Igman and Bjelasnica in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the very page. The previous one was only put on the screen so that you could be able to see that it was May 1996. You heard this from Major Mamlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That refers to that incident, I believe. However, there is another reference to it contemporaneously, but this accurately also reflects the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope you didn't hold these sharp words against me.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I mean you're just a reflection on the truth, that is, that I report the truth as I hear it, and that's what Major Mamlic had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, this part of this page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When we admit part of this article we'll also admit the cover page as well in order to follow what it is about. So we will admit this page and the previous page in order to find who Mr. Djurdjevic was meeting with. So we'll admit three pages as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When mentioned that Perisic thought that Milosevic had made a mistake by having accepted me to hold the position I had in Bosnia, do you agree that despite mutual respect, Milosevic and I were ideologically opposed and that he did not appoint me in any way? I did not even run for the position in 1990, and he never came to terms with the fact that in Bosnia there was this centrist government.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I quite follow the gist of the question, but I will try my best to answer this way: When you and I first met, which was in 1992, I did have the impression that the interests of Milosevic and your government at the time were closely aligned; in other words, at the outset of the war. Then as time went on and subsequent meetings, Milosevic began to shift and change, and by that stage, even by 1992, I had already concluded after several meetings with him that he was a turncoat Communist, that he could not be trusted to stay the course. And it was just a matter of time, in my own opinion, as to when he would begin to shift and change his positions. When that happened, and the first sign of that happened actually in the summer of 1994 when he buckled under the Western pressure and sanctions and imposed the sanctions against the Bosnian Serb Republic, that was a clear public sign of falling out between the leadership of the two Serbian factions: The one in the former Yugoslavia in Belgrade and the leadership in the Bosnian Serb Republic. So I don't really know how you got to be in the position of president of the Bosnian Serb Republic. I was not intimately familiar or following the war back in 1994 from the Sarajevo standpoint. All I know is from what Professor Koljevic had told me, that you had not really volunteered for that, that you were kind of pushed to do that, that you accepted the responsibility and took the meddle because you felt that your nation was in danger of being overrun when the country of Yugoslavia began to fall apart. But just exactly who approved whom and how you got to be there, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps then there's no point in asking you whether you could observe that during any elections President Milosevic always supported our opposition, including Biljana Plavsic once she became our political enemy.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: To which elections are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Starting with 1996 onwards, as long as he was alive. Let me remind you, he supported Ivanic against Krajisnik. He supported Drago Ilic, his socialist party member as well as Zivko Radisic. He supported Biljana and Dodik. They were always our opponents. He never supported us.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I actually didn't know that but it's entirely consistent with everything I knew about the man, and it's consistent with that comment that Perisic had made. Perisic then being his -- Milosevic's chief of the army, and it is also consistent with my perception of Milosevic as the man who even in our first meeting in January 1990 when the Soviet Union was still standing, looking strong, did not fully understand how the game of geopolitics is played. And I was going to say that by 1996, he has certainly lost his compass, but now that I think back about that, meaning in January 1990, I don't think he ever had a compass that worked when it came to global politics and geopolitics, and so he was, I think, always go -- he was always going by his gut feel. And when he felt the headwinds were too strong, he would turn the other way. So it's not surprising he supported your opposition in 1996, even though you were very closely working together and collaborating in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjevic, let us reach July 1995 as quickly as we can. Is it correct that you had to choose the route you would take and that between Zvornik and Pale you took the longer road, which was in poorer condition because the main road was dangerous to travel along because of the combat which took place on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You met Professor Koljevic. Had you met him before that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have met him before. I believe the first time in 1993, but this was the first time that I had really spent an extended time with him, like several hours, all evening. We had dinner together, too, and also a good part of the following morning. So it was really the first time that I spent a long time with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Professor Koljevic was an exceptional personality, especially in terms of the humane side of his nature? He was quite positively disposed towards Muslims and Croatia, especially when it came to their humanitarian needs.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: There's no question that that's true. Professor Koljevic gave the appearance and came across as a person who wouldn't hurt a fly. He was completely harmless, and he was a very caring man. When we were talking about that night when momentous events were taking place on the ground in Srebrenica, the night of July 13th, he was very excited to be able to go there the following day, looking forward to going there the following day to extend his hand of friendship to the Muslims in Srebrenica and to promise them, to assure them that they would be treated the same way by the Bosnian Serb government as were the Serbian civilians. And if you followed my war diary from that point on, unfortunately that never happened, because by that stage all the civilians had been evacuated from Srebrenica by General Mladic and the trucks that he had laid on. But professor -- if Professor Koljevic had his way, he would have held a press conference there on the 14th of July to announce to the world how magnanimous the Serbian government is and to ensure the civilians of Srebrenica that they had nothing to fear. That is what he had told me at the time, but as I said, that never came to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, was Professor Koljevic the right person to be in charge of the co-ordinating body and committee in charge of co-operation with UNPROFOR and other humanitarian organisations? Was there anyone better than him in our -- among our leaders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, in all fairness, only you can answer that question. I don't know all the people that you had at your disposal. All I can say is that Professor Koljevic, to me, seemed very appropriate for the job, if for no other reason because he spoke excellent English. He was a scholar, he was not a soldier, and therefore he instilled a certain amount of respect in people that he was dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 65 ter 22306. On page 21, you discuss a possible departure of Professor Koljevic and yourself for Srebrenica. Was it your impression that both Professor Koljevic and I believed that at least the local population of Srebrenica would not leave, that they would choose to stay and that there was reason enough for you to go to Srebrenica? Page 21, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: The answer to your question is yes. That's clearly the impression I had the night of the 13th when I witnessed first-hand the conversation that Professor Koljevic had on the phone with you, in which he outlined to you his plan to go to Srebrenica, the plan that I've just explained, to show goodwill toward the Muslim civilians. And as for your concurrence with that plan, you did concur. You did agree. So the impression I got was that two of you were thinking alike, that you were on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know at the time that in addition to the local population in Srebrenica there were many refugees from the nearby municipalities, and was it your impression that we did count on some people leaving but that we hoped that most of the local population would stay? In other words, were you able to observe a difference of position or intention between those refugees and the locals? It's at the top of the page: [In English] "But there was still hope that they --" [Interpretation] Does this refer to our expectations that a sufficient number of civilians would remain behind so as to be able to take care of them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: To answer your first question, no, I could not make a distinction between a domestic and refugees. I didn't know that that was the case, and we never discussed -- Professor Koljevic and I never discussed that distinction. We just talked about the civilian population in general in Srebrenica. And as for the second question, yes, it's a bit of a contradiction here, because on the 13th, the night of the 13th, in our conversation at Professor Koljevic's office, he had already told me, as well as his Chief of Cabinet, that Mladic [Realtime transcript read in error "Milosevic"] had evacuated all civilians and yet both he and you had held out hope that we would still be able to go, perhaps because you thought that the domestic population was still there. I don't know that. But clearly the morning of the 14th, as you see in this transcript, Professor Koljevic and I had still intended to go to Srebrenica figuring that there are some civilians left. However, that changed at some point later on that day when it became obvious that that would be pointless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Djurdjevic, could you check whether any part in the beginning of your answer is missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, this immediate answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would make the trip. That's the missing part. There's still hope that they would make the trip.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think his Excellency thinks of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 44.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, excuse me. First of all, there's a mistake here. It says "Milosevic" when we're talking Mladic. Milosevic had nothing to do with Srebrenica evacuations. That's the first mistake. And in then in the continuation it says, "... had evacuated all civilians but that you" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So did you begin your answer with, "That was the case?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you back up the transcript a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. See if I can figure it out. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's fine. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Yes. I had the impression that you started answering the question while the interpretation was going on, but that can be looked into later on. Yes.
