utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe you said that was the case when you referred to what I said, that there was still hope of some civilians being there; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the lack of information, do you agree that you were able to observe that at the time it was impossible to establish telephone communication and that you, too, had serious problems when trying to arrange meetings with me or Mladic and that was the reason why we had incomplete information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I can say is definitely true, that all day that I had spent at your office on July 14th, the secure lines were down and that I could not communicate with General Mladic, with whom I was trying to set up a meeting, because my primary purpose, actually, for that trip in July 1995 was to meet with him. When he couldn't make it on our appointed time on July 13th, he had sent General Gvero to meet with me instead, and his officers have said that he would try to make time for us to meet the following day, which was the 14th, and that I was to call to see when and where we could meet. So all day long I had been trying to -- they gave me the number to use for the secure lines to do that. So all day long I've been trying to call that, the secure lines, and all day long they were down. And I know that also I witnessed -- I know that you and your office have both the open and secure lines and that you were not able to communicate on the secure lines either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards directive number 7, or my order number 7, is it possible that you wanted to know what this operation was about and what was going on in Eastern Bosnia, and that's how it came to be that directive number 7 was mentioned? Is it possible that you were interested in finding out what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I recall is that that directive number 7, order number 7, came up in the context of our discussion when you said that the objective of the military campaign is to bring things to a boiling point, and my impression was that you were letting me know that the initiative, i.e., the order, had come from you. What directive number 7 was, I have no idea. I just remember you mentioning that reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it have been mentioned in the context of your queries about any disagreements between the military and civilian structures in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that would be the proper context, because then immediately after that we had got into the conversation that I actually did want to have with you about the disagreements between the military leaders, Mladic in particular, and your government in which you had shared with me the information that was new to me at the time. And that is that in collusion with Milosevic, I believe in April of that year, April of 1995, General Mladic was planning to stage sort of a coup d'etat to displace you as the head of government and that you had gone to the military leadership whom you had assembled and faced them up with that information to -- about which you said that many of these officers were completely taken aback and surprised to learn that. You then also told me that you had asked Mladic to come to your office for a private meeting in which you had asked him to set three hours aside to carry out, and you said that in that meeting you had once again asserted your authority as the chief commander, as civilian commander, Commander-in-Chief, and that -- you know, I got the impression -- you got the impression that therefore that rift had been smoothed out. However, before I left your office that evening, as we were leaving, you said something that made me wonder about that, because you said, I think we're going to need to pension Mladic off. And that's what got me the impression that perhaps things were smoothed out at the surface, but deep down there were still differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now call up 65 ter 16077, page 37 in e-court. And that page you speak about that. Did you see that our misunderstandings did not concern crimes but only the concept of civilian control, and did you see for yourself that I had the impression that I did not have enough control over the military?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, do I need to look at the exhibit before answering that, or can I just answer it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means. If necessary, please take a look at whatever pages you want to. Shall we show you the first page --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at the first page. It starts with the words "Koljevic," and so on, and "visit to Srebrenica," and then it's on page 36. Yes. That should be the right page, the one that we have now. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [In English] Yes, I do remember. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, this is not the right page now. The next one, please. Ask for it to scroll down when you need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to ensure that we understand this in context, and that is we correctly understand that it is the accused's case that whatever conflict or tensions existed between himself and General Mladic had nothing to do with crimes but had to do instead with some other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I understand he's drawing -- he's asking the witness to draw a conclusion in that regard based on -- on his presentation of that dichotomy, and I just want to make sure that's properly understood if that indeed is his case to the witness and before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Maybe this is a good time to just visit this issue of what is our case, because every time Dr. Karadzic puts a factual assertion to a witness, he's being asked whether that's his case or not, and that's not what we're doing. It's not our case every time we're testing the witness with some factual assertion. Our case is that the Prosecution hasn't proved that the crimes that are charged against Dr. Karadzic as to each and every element and that we're not going to say anything in this courtroom at any time during the trial that will relieve the Prosecution of the burden of proving each and every element of each and every charge. So there's nothing in Dr. Karadzic's questions that he puts to a witness that is intended or should be used to relieve the Prosecution of their burden of proof of anything in the trial. That starts with wither anybody was killed in Srebrenica, the reasons for why they were killed, who may have killed them, why Dr. Karadzic did what he did, whether he punished and for what reason. All of those things -- nothing that we are doing during this part of the case when we're questioning witnesses is intended to assist the Prosecutor to relieve him of the burden of proving all of the aspects of the case. So I think it's -- I wanted to make that clear because this keeps coming up. So it's not Dr. Karadzic's case that he didn't punish General Mladic for crimes or that he didn't want to punish General Mladic for crimes or that their disagreements had nothing to do with crimes. That's not our case. And it doesn't relieve the Prosecution of the burden with respect to the issue of Dr. Karadzic's knowledge of any crimes of Mladic or failure to punish those crimes. So I hope I help the Court with that intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, speaking for myself, Mr. Robinson, not really. Nobody is suggesting that the queries are designed to relieve the burden upon the Prosecution, which is plain and straightforward. But it's very useful to know during extended cross-examinations when the Court is being required to sift matters what it is that they are being asked to conclude, and it is not very helpful if the Court isn't given that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may just add one point. That's part of what underlies the submission I made a moment ago. Of course, Prosecution never shrinks from its duty and is happy to embrace it. That's Mr. Robinson stating the truism about the Prosecution's burden of proof doesn't address the issue at all. And to expand on the point that His Honour Judge Morrison just made, that issue is further amplified when the accused not only obscures what is being addressed to a witness but affirmatively stakes out a position that is apparently the basis for the proposition being put to the witness and the assertions impliedly being made, and that's why I raise the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the question that triggered your intervention was whether witness saw that our -- I quote: "Did you see that our misunderstanding did not concern crimes but only the concept of civilian control ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the original trigger for this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll resolve this in this way: I'll ask you, Mr. Karadzic, to clarify what you meant when you say "crimes": "Did you see that our misunderstanding did not concern crimes but only the concept of civilian control?" What did you mean? Do you consider there were crimes that were committed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You're right. All of you are right. I'm going to be much clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, did you see for yourself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please clarify to the Court. We put the question. Please answer to us. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I thought you were asking me to redefine my question, to put a clearer question. This is what I meant: Did the witness know that I knew of some crimes, and was my dissatisfaction with the military due to some crime or was this a doctrinary conflict because of control? I'll explain that in my next question. So to the best of this witness's knowledge, what was the reason for the misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will, we'll leave it at that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you -- actually, it's obvious here, isn't it, that I said that the army had to be an instrument of the state, not a state in its own right? Can we now have the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go any further, is this exhibit -- document the same one we looked at during the in chief? But why is the page number different? This is -- this is a document of 113 pages, and one we looked at is of only 70 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe I can explain that. Two of the two versions of "War Drums are Beating," the trip journal from July 5th to July 31st were uploaded. One, the longer version, encompasses the entire trip. However, portions of that trip took place after the witness left Bosnia and went on to Western Europe and there are also some articles attached to that that are part of that same journal. So because it wasn't clear whether -- how they would be used and whether the focus would be as expected on the Bosnian portion or the Bosnian and Serbian portion of the trip, we thought we would give the Court and the parties sufficient flexibility by uploading both the entirety of that trip diary and only that portion, the shortened portion, that related to the trip within Serbia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So this 65 ter number 16077 is a longer version of 65 ter 6972. I put it for the record, and let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to take a look at the first three or four paragraphs of these notes of yours. Do you agree or do you remember that I complained about the following: As far as humanitarian aid is concerned I spent more time talking to my own people rather than our adversaries, and I complained that Professor Koljevic was not given due respect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did get the impression that what was at stake here was a power play as to who is in charge. I have never discussed with you or with Mladic, for that matter, issues of crimes being committed because I was not aware of any at that time. And it's also accurate what you said, that you told me that Professor Koljevic had to spend more time negotiating with his own army the permissions to -- for the UNPROFOR convoys to pass and that that was unnecessary and humiliating for someone in the position like Professor Koljevic, who was the representative of the civilian government in that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it quite clear to you, Mr. Djurdjevic, that both Koljevic and I were in favour of allowing the largest possible quantities of humanitarian aid to be delivered in an unhindered way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So as for this paragraph entitled "Mladic's coup d'etat," could that be admitted in full?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Should we add that to the pre-existing Prosecution exhibit, or do you like to be kept as a separate Defence exhibit? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It can be added. That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be added to Exhibit P4515.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although you've already given an answer, I would like to be clearer in respect of that confusing question of mine that made the Prosecutor react. Did you see for yourself -- actually, did you think that I knew of any crimes, and did you have any awareness of crimes, and did you think that we had any awareness of crimes at the time when we had this clash with the military?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: My answer is no. I just said in my previous comment that I was not aware of any crimes at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on this page, can we scroll down and then can we tender the entire page later. You remember that during the offensive against Sarajevo, my daughter's wedding took place, and you say here that I asked elderly people whether we should postpone the wedding, and they said that we shouldn't do that. Is it correct what you say here, that it should not be postponed but, rather, should be carried through?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm everything that I've said in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Within that framework, as you lived in the diaspora, in a democratic world, and also on the basis of your own experience, did you come to the conclusion that I was an autocrat; or, on the contrary, did you think that people could talk to me, could tell me the truth? Do you not refer to that here? Look at what this -- this -- this Miocic, I think, says: [In English] "... said because most people around Radovan Karadzic are hoping to get ahead by kissing up to him, rather than telling him the truth. Yet RK is a kind of a person to whom you can tell the truth, and he won't bite your head off for it." [Interpretation] Those were his words, right, that the truth can be told to me? Did you see that for yourself? And on the whole, the democratic diaspora, did they all have some impression of me? Did you personally have some impression of me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad you added this last part, because I can't speak for the diaspora. Yes, I do with what you said, and, yes, I did put that theory to the test when I asked you the testy question about your daughter's wedding, which was actually brought to my attention by General Perisic first in our meeting in Belgrade before this trip when he spoke about you disparagingly, that here you were in the middle of the war and a major offensive taking place and you and your daughter and the wedding guests were partying. That's how, to paraphrase, he had put it. So I put that to a test and you explained just like I said in this -- in my notes, that you had asked for opinions of elders in your community and they counselled you to have a wedding but to keep it quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remind me again of who ZM referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. ZM is the initials of the Chief of Cabinet for Professor Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You said that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 11. 65 ter 23636. I hope that this entire page, then, will be admitted under the number that had already been assigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In hard copy it's page 11, and I don't know what page it is in e-court. Can we go to where it says page 11. Ah, yes, that's fine. Could you please focus on this bit, "Truth and Communist Officers in RS." Is that what you were saying in relation to Igman, and, generally speaking, that once we took upon ourselves certain obligations we had to honour them at any cost?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly it. In our previous reference to that, we used my discussion with Major Mamlic, and, if you recall, that's when I said there had been other references to that same incident in my diary, and this is exactly it. This is the one I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be added as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be added to Exhibit P4518.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, let us not expose ourselves to the danger of the Prosecution assisting the Defence. Can we have the previous page, just for the sake of identification. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, you've already spoken about this, but when was the first time that you heard of some killings in relation to Srebrenica? Did you learn anything about that while you were in Pale, and when did you hear about it in general? And from whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: After my visit to Bosnia in July 1995, as Mr. Tieger had pointed out, I continued my trip out of the country. I went to Vienna, and then from Vienna to Germany, and then to Poland, I believe, travelling with my daughter from that point onwards, from Vienna onwards, and I do believe that it was at some point in Germany. I recall that we were in church - It could have been in Berlin, I'm not a hundred per cent sure which church and just exactly where - where I saw a poster talking about a massacre in Srebrenica, and they were collecting donations for the victims in Srebrenica. Because we were travelling, I had not really kept up with it hour-by-hour or day-by-day news, and besides, I rarely watch TV anyway for the reasons we've already discussed before, so that was the first time that I recall that I'd become aware of anything to do with alleged crimes being committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I just need to check a few things and then I'll go back to ... During this time that we spent together on the 14th of July, you observed that there was a delegation there from Srebrenica, the civilian authorities of Srebrenica visiting me, headed by Mr. Deronjic. Do you remember that I informed you that we had talked to that delegation about technical matters pertaining to civilian control and authority in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that during day I went from one room to another and then yet another one, because at the same time I had several different visitors? And did I ask you also to excuse me because I had to leave you every now and then in order to see other visitors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall you leaving me in your office and going out to do other things, but, yes, I do remember the comings and goings all day long in and out of your office, different people coming in, going out, and this delegation from Srebrenica was, I believe, just leaving as our meeting had commenced. And there were quite a few of them. I don't remember exactly how many, but it was more than just a mayor that -- or would-be mayor that you were meeting with. So, yes, you were one busy man on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that someone informed me of the fighting in the northern part of the area. Do we agree that this was on the 14th and that fighting was far away from Srebrenica, to the north, in the direction of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I recall is that you took a phone call from someone, some military commander, telling you that there is fighting going on as the column -- alleged a large column of 10.000 or so Muslim fighters was trying to make their way from Srebrenica toward Tuzla. Just where exactly that was I don't know. I don't think you told me or anyone else has. But your response to that was, Oh, it is probably more like 2- or 3.000. In other words, you felt the commander was exaggerating the strength of the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, I'm intervening because I had the impression that Mr. Karadzic was moving away from this topic, but in answer to his question that -- I quote: "Do you remember that I inform --" it's about his meeting with the mayor, Mr. Deronjic. I quote: "Do you remember that I informed you that we had talked to that delegation about technical matters pertaining to civilian control and authority in Srebrenica?" And your answer was: "Yes, I do remember that." What are those technical matters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware of the details of that conversation, because I was not present there. I walked into his office just as that delegation had left. I can only surmise it had to do with the establish of a civilian authority because they had just militarily taken that city and the technical matters to me meant logistical issues to do with setting up the government there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what Mr. Karadzic told you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you want the exact quote, could we go back to my diary as of that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We'll find this page now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. You want to be on -- it's page 34 of the hard copy, which I believe is page -- I can check on my notes. Page 30 -- probably page -- I'd try page 36 of the e-court. That's if we're talking about 4615.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we try page 35. No, we -- okay. Is this it now? Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you can scroll up, I think that's at least one of the references you had in mind. Up by I mean higher in the page, not lower in the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Do you read that part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it now. Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I guess it don't shed any more light in regards the specific terminology. So as best as I can recall, what I told you is exactly what he had said. My impression was that they were setting -- trying to set up the civilian government in Srebrenica and that that's what these technical issues and logistical discussions were about. This also corroborates what Professor Koljevic had told me, that it was his intention, if you recall, the day before and the morning of July 14th, to go there as a representative of the civilian government and with his presence accomplish the same, to carry the message that the local civilians will be dealt with fairly by the Serbian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And probably Mr. Robinson will advise you, Mr. Karadzic. While you are entitled to put leading questions to the Prosecution witness to strengthen the probative value of evidence you are going to get from the witness, it's better for you to let the witness say the words. I note the time. It's time to take a break for half an hour, we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjevic, do we agree that in the course of the interview we had, you confirmed that I did not get involved in your work. I didn't try to influence your work as a journalist, and my associates didn't do this either. In brief, did you gain the impression that I was in favour of freedom of speech, in favour of the media having access to accurate information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: The short answer is yes. I have never felt pressured in any way and always felt free to speak and write what I saw and felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can continue, yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Excellency, for your well-intentioned suggestions, but since it's quite difficult to advise me, because sometimes the questions I put are moral rather than legal -- well, as a result, I would like Mr. Robinson to put several questions to Mr. Djurdjevic, questions that he is better placed to phrase than I am, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to that, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to create an unnecessary problem if this is some kind of one-off exception that doesn't erode the general principles under which we've been operating, but I frankly -- it's a very vague explanation, and I can't quite understand exactly why this exceptional approach is required and why the accused doesn't continue with his -- I don't know the nature of the subject matters that would require that, and if there is a legal submission to be made which is normally the province of Mr. Robinson, I can't understand why it's being put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you help us in that regard, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are some questions, actually only two, that I really believe very important that this witness be asked concerning Dr. Karadzic and the issue of what did he know and when did he know it, which to me is most important issue in the Srebrenica part of the case. And Dr. Karadzic, when we discussed it, he is uncomfortable asking these questions sometimes himself. I have to tell you that frequently we disagree about whether he should be defending the Serb people, as he likes to do, or defending himself, as I think he should do. This is one issue where he -- we -- I felt that there are some questions that would really assist him in defending himself, and I think he feels more comfortable if I put those questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I know I've said it before, but I can't resist saying it again: The Serb people are not on trial, Serbian culture is not on trial. So with the greatest of respect, your view, Mr. Robinson, as to the object of the trial is preferable. I just find the concept of Dr. Karadzic being shy is not immediately easy to encompass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, did you say two topics? Two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two questions, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said, this is for the purpose of the transcript, that sometimes I give priority to moral issues rather than to legal ones. It wasn't that I put moral questions. And that is why it is difficult to advise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, the two questions that you have in mind that you want to ask, would it be possible for you to put those words -- to put your words in Dr. Karadzic's mouth so that the question, the very question that you want to ask, he would ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I can easily do that. I have them written down. I can hand him the piece of paper and he can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: If this would not be a problem, would it be possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It would be possible, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would resolve everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, in the course of our meeting, in the course of your stay in Pale and Republika Srpska, did you have any information according to which prisoners from Srebrenica should be killed or according to which prisoners from Srebrenica were killed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: As I've already testified, during that visit during July 1995, I do not recall any knowledge of crimes being committed of any kind, of the prisoners being executed or the civilians. These are the allegations and charges of which I became aware after the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And my second question now. Given what you knew about me, given what you think about me, would you say that I wanted to inflict harm on innocent victims, that I wanted innocent victims to be killed, prisoners, civilians, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I object to that question. That goes well beyond the province of any witness, particularly a fact witness offering, sort of, speculations about the inner workings of -- and possibilities or potentialities of the accused with respect to crimes. And maybe if that's going to be the rule, maybe we are going to start asking questions of witnesses who have encountered Dr. Karadzic in other circumstances about what they think, based on what they know, if he's capable of such crimes. I'm sure those questions would be objected to, and I'm sure those questions would be sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the question he intended was: Did he have any inkling from his visit to Pale on the 13th and 14th of July, 1995, that Dr. Karadzic favoured the commission of any such crimes, and I think he could answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was asked and answered earlier in respect of -- at page 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 28.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's now been correctly interpreted "inclined," whereas my question was not properly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will allow the question as reformulated by Mr. Robinson. Do you remember the question, Mr. Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and my answer is based on everything I have known about Dr. Karadzic and my opinions I've formed on him, and specifically what I have seen and witnessed on July 13th and 14th, 1995, in my visits there in Bosnia, I cannot conceive a circumstance where Dr. Karadzic would be party to any such crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, let me return to a page reference that I made just a moment ago. That was at page 28, where you indicated in response to a question about your impressions, Dr. Karadzic and his policy, that they were formed in part about the fact that you heard Dr. Karadzic -- that your answer was, "On the contrary, I heard you condemn any acts of violence against your enemies" was part of the answer. And I wanted to ask you this question: Did you ever hear Dr. Karadzic personally or via other sources condemn the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, as I've just said, at the time I was with Dr. Karadzic, I was not aware of any murders of either prisoners or civilians. I hadn't learned about these allegations only after I had left Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I heard at that answer, sir, and I certainly appreciate that. My question is slightly different. You testified about hearing Dr. Karadzic condemn crimes which you indicated as part of your basis for forming your impression of him. I'm asking if you ever heard him condemn crimes in Srebrenica and specifically the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean subsequently to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You referred to -- Mr. Djurdjevic, to order number 7. Did you, yourself, have the opportunity to read it at a later stage, directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I still have no idea what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DJURDJEVIC
utterances.text: Lucky number 7, but I don't know. It's purely speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, you are -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We usually do not hear from the witness but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to, first of all, say, to commend you for the work you are doing here, and I hope that you realise that the work that's being done in this courtroom goes well beyond the Balkans, and if the full truth and reconciliation can take place in this perennially troubled region, it could serve as a model for conflict resolution elsewhere in Iraq, in Afghanistan, in Somalia. And it's my hope and prayer when your work is done, that that's the legacy that you leave behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjevic. On behalf of this Chamber as well as the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now, you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It seems that whoever was bringing the next witness scheduled it on the basis of the allocated times. I understand the witness won't be arriving until approximately 10 after 1.00. I might note that meanwhile, Mr. Mitchell might be able to raise a small matter that he intended to, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You recall last night with Mr. Manning there was some discussion about a particular blindfold and whether or not it had a knot to it, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On which he indicated arrow or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. The proper full-sized version of that has now been uploaded into e-court and given 65 ter 23646. So I'd like to tender that if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we upload it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. Now, while that's coming up, Mr. President, Mr. Manning actually said at transcript page 25878 he was being asked questions about -- my apologies, 23647.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this stay here, too, so that we can see that it's on the forehead, not covering the eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, what I was going to come to, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- yes. Could we rotate 270 degrees. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I was going to suggest, Mr. President, that we tender -- there's actually four items I'd like to tender, this shot in the grave, the photo from the morgue, which is 23647 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we look at them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly. So this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. So if we can now go to 23647. If we can -- this is the photo that we looked at yesterday. We can rotate it back 90 degrees to the left. That's the angle we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first picture was taken where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then this was taken at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. So the first photo was taken by Mr. Peccerelli and his team. This photo was taken at the morgue by Dr. Clark and his team. Now, the next photo is 23648, and this is the material once it's been taken off and washed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the last one is -- and this was something that Mr. Manning was specifically asked to see, which was the autopsy report, to see its description, and that's 23649. And this was one of the autopsies that was overseen by Dr. John Clark. You can see both in the summary and also in the body it describes the strip of cloth that was knotted behind and there was some issue - this is how it first came up - whether there was a knot or not behind the head, and Mr. Manning actually asked to see the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we upload two at the same time, the first two photos, one taken from the grave and one taken at the morgue. I'm not sure if it is possible. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's 23646 and -647.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. We rotate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Mr. President, the reason we know this is the same body is you can see the LZ 01-596 tag on both bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 596. As Mr. Karadzic indicated, that is strip is on his forehead in the grave, but was it changed at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think Mr. Manning and everybody testified that -- all these experts testified that these artefacts would move during transport --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's why they were photographed and logged at every stage. So, you know, these photos explain exactly where the blindfold was in the grave, where it was at the morgue, and its description. I can't offer you any more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Fair enough. Any objections to admission of these four items?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, apart from the fact that I think that the autopsy findings don't relate to this, because we are looking for a ribbon that was sewn or was of a piece, not something that was tied into a knot, because the one -- the findings in the autopsy refer to a ribbon that was tied into a knot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's different. It's a separate issue from admitting it, but just given the time we still have, could we take a look at the autopsy report, 23649. I think there's a passage that he was blindfolded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think if we go to -- that's the summary on the front page. You can go to page 5 in e-court, which are the handwritten notes of the pathologist who did the examination. And down the bottom of the page under "Blindfold," that's the description that was given at the time the body was on the autopsy table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So those four items will be admitted separately or in one item. They are separated. We'll admit them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: They're separate items, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 23646 will be Exhibit P4519; 65 ter 23647 will be Exhibit P4520; 65 ter 23648 will be Exhibit P4521; and 65 ter 23649 will be Exhibit P4522.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we adjourn for 15 minutes? That's the best course of action. We will resume at quarter past. --- Break taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, just to let you know, we have approximately 30 minutes left before we have to adjourn, so I don't want you to be startled by the what may otherwise seem like the abrupt conclusion of today as we're going through your testimony, but we'll try to cover as much ground as we can. First of all, would you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct, sir, that you have appeared before this Tribunal previously and, in particular, in September of 2007, from the 17th to the 19th, when you testified in the case of Popovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 22391.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And while that is being called up, ask you, sir, whether you have had the opportunity to review your testimony in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. I listened to the CD, and I heard all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that you have certain clarifications you wanted to make to that that you brought to our attention and that we memorialised and also provided to the Defence. If I can just cite for them you and if you can confirm if it's an accurate understanding of the corrections or clarifications you wanted to make. The first was at -- although I know you made them with respect to the audio, it is reflected at page 15465 of the transcript where you corrected the date when you joined the VRS, which was 17 December 1993, not 17 November 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The second is that, and this is reflected at page 15521, that you used the word "responsibility," but did not use the word "responsibility" in a legal sense but instead in the sense of a job or duty or role; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And more specifically, as indicated in the supplemental information sheet, that appears or is reflected at page 15521, line 23, and 15522, line 6. Moving on to the next one, this is reflected at page 15540. You explained that the office for co-operation with foreign military representatives was not in the cabinet of the Main Staff. It was actually under the immediate control of the commander of the Main Staff but separate from the cabinet. And is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next one is reflected at page 15545 at line 6, and you explained that Tomo Kovac was not minister of defence. He was minister of the interior. Is that also a correction you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next is reflected at pages 15475, beginning at line 24 and continuing on to page 15476, line 1. That regards the 12 July 1995 document, which is 65 ter 01887 in this case, and you explained that that document is actually addressed to the -- addressed to the Secretariat of Defence of Zvornik, not originating from there, and that would be clear if you could see the Ministry of Defence header. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is true as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally at page 15468, line 23, to page 15469 line 2, you wanted to clarify a matter of who your superior was at any given time, and you explained that from 17 December 1993 to 24 July 1994, your immediate superior was Grujo Boric; and from 24 July 1994 until after the end of the war, your immediate superior was the head of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic. And is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one thing. He was not the chief [Realtime transcript read in error "commander"] of the Main Staff but the commander [Realtime transcript read in error "chief"] of the Main Staff. The rest of the information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, with those clarifications, can you confirm that 65 ter 22391, your testimony in the Popovic case, accurately reflects your statement at the time and is accurate information and that if asked about those same matters here in court, you would provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 22391 and the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll first admit the transcript in the Popovic et al. case. Give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4523, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A few questions with regard to associated exhibits. 65 ter number 1886 -- oh, yes. No problem. What was the point of 15442, instruction about contacts with international organisation? It's transcript page 15543. Very well. All of the associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence and be given numbers in due course by the Registry. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would like to call your attention to 30925B which is an intercept that should be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will read a very brief summary and then move on to some additional questions. General, these summaries are not intended to capture the totality of the information provided in your testimony but just a brief picture of what that was. In 1995, the witness was assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel of the Main Staff in the VRS. His -- he was directly subordinated to General Ratko Mladic. He testified about the structure and organisation of the Main Staff and of aspects of the VRS. The witness also testified that on the evening of 11 July 1995, he received an order that originated from General Mladic to organise buses and, among other things, conveyed to the Ministry of Defence a request for buses to be provided also by the Ministry of the Defence. He spoke with Momcilo -- Mojmilo Kovacevic of the Ministry of Defence by telephone and then in writing subsequently on 12 July. The witness also testified about a meeting with the accused he attended on 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, the Trial Chamber has before it your Popovic testimony which details your background and your various positions within the military. As you explained in Popovic, your work on the Main Staff beginning in 1994 was as assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation and personnel. Now, you further explained at transcript 14468 that the organisation had basically been established by the time you arrived. You explained at 15468 what mobilisation entailed and the extent to which the Ministry of Defence was involved in responsibility for call-up papers and so on. And you also explained that personnel entailed, among other things, the education of officers, assignments, preparation of documents for promotion, reassignment, decorations, and so on. So I'd just like to show you one document perhaps by way of understanding at least some aspects of your personnel duties, and if I could quickly call up 65 ter 03739. General, this is a document from you dated December 25, 1994, which was pursuant to the order of the commander of the VRS. That's General Mladic; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this -- is it correct that this document concerns staffing or bringing to establishment the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska; that you are pursuing the transfer of six soldiers, two of whom are from the Hercegovina Corps, four are from the Drina Corps to be transferred to the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It concerned the bringing up to establishment levels of the 10th Sabotage Detachment pursuant to the order of the commander of the VRS. So it concerned staffing levels. The people mentioned in the document were being transferred to the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And under whose -- what -- was the 10th Sabotage Detachment under a corps or was it -- it refers here to the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska. Is the -- does that mean that the 10th Sabotage Detachment is directly under General Mladic's command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as the order indicates, it says "pursuant to the order of the commander." Is it correct that you received that order and then implemented it for the commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I refer to that particular number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4524, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could I draw your attention to transcript page today 73, lines -- lines 15 to 17. In answer to your question whether Mladic was his immediate superior, was the head of Main Staff, the witness was recorded to answer like this, but I'm not sure whether it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a very good catch because I understood it to be -- his clarification to be a bit different as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your answer is like this, General, so could you clarify: "I would like to clarify one thing. He was not commander of the Main Staff but Chief of the Main Staff. The rest of the information is accurate." There must be something wrong. Do you remember answering that question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. I simply switched the term. He was not the Chief of the Main Staff but the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I believe that some of your previous answers suggested this, but I want to clarify both your role and the role of other assistant commanders. So could -- could you as assistant commander take steps to deal with the corps, the Drina Corps, the Hercegovina Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, and so on, could you take those steps without the approval of the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you found that someone was not following correct procedure or not following the orders that you had made pursuant to orders of the commander, did you directly deal with those persons or did you report it to the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When there were problems, we reported them to the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you alluded to this earlier, that assistant commanders implement -- well, you implemented the orders of the commander of the Main Staff. Is it also true of the other assistant commanders in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I am familiar with their competencies, I believe the same practice was followed by the other assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And would you say and have you said that assistant commanders were experts at implementing General Mladic's orders?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, at the top of this hierarchy of command and control, who is at the very top of that, of that hierarchy, starting at the bottom with the lowliest soldier up to the top level of exercising command and control? No, just in -- in the overall structure of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In the Army of Republika Srpska, the army commander was the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Ratko Mladic. However, at the helm of the armed forces of the VRS, which includes the army and members of the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say the police, is the supreme commander, the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. So the first strategic level is the republican president. The second level is the command of the Main Staff. The third level were the corps commanders, and so on and so forth, down to the simple soldiers. That was the hierarchical structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me turn now to something you testified about in the Popovic case, and you indicated that in July of 1995, you were posted at the rear command post in Han Pijesak, and discussed at page 15468 of the Popovic transcript -- excuse me. That was discussed at page 15468. Let me perhaps assist by calling up 65 ter 01913. This is a document that was discussed during the course of your testimony in Popovic, and you -- and let me just indicate what the document is quickly. It's a 12 July 1995 document directed to the Ministry of Defence that indicates with the utmost urgency order of the Sarajevo and Zvornik Ministry of Defence secretariats to mobilise through various municipalities all buses available. At least 50 buses need to be mobilised and must be sent to Bratunac sports stadium by a certain time on the 12th of July at the latest. Now, General, you explained at pages -- at page 15472 of the Popovic testimony that this resulted from your telephone call the evening before with -- first with someone from the Main Staff and then with the Ministry of Defence, and explained also that the order to do so emanated from General Mladic. That was at page 15473. I'd like to ask you just a few questions before we break about that. First of all, with respect to the phone call that you received from the Main Staff, can you tell us approximately when you received it on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was late in the evening that I received the phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So on page 1873 -- let me ask you for some clarification on that. I know at page 18731 of your testimony in the Tolimir case, you refer to the afternoon and then most probably the evening hours. So is it correct we're talking about sometime in the -- not necessarily the afternoon but sometime around evening?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a better way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did -- did -- is what you received, was that a request or an order? In other words, were you instructed or ordered to take steps with respect to this -- to the buses?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I received an order. It was conveyed to me as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm not asking you who conveyed the order, but from whom did that order come? Who was the source of that order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how you knew that the order -- understanding you didn't speak directly with General Mladic, how you knew that the order came from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in principle, I know that such orders could not arrive from anyone other than the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic. That was one thing. Another thing, it was a phone call, and it was the specific phone which only received phone calls from the commander. I believe in the Tolimir case I stated it was line number 250. Therefore, that was sufficient indication that the order arrived from the commander of the Main Staff. If you're interested in any names, I'll gladly explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally General, did the person who called you from extension 250 inform you that it was a decision by the commander, General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, as I indicated we were going to adjourn at approximately this time, so I will leave it with that last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll rise for today and resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of March, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
